lead: A strain gauge is a resistor glued to a part. When the part stretches or compresses, the resistor changes resistance in proportion to the strain. The constant of proportionality is the gauge factor. This simple idea turns a mechanical quantity into an electrical one. Engineers use it for load cells, pressure diaphragms, torque shafts and displacement beams. It also measures bone strain, implant load, muscle force and breathing. The next sections separate the mechanics from the resistor, compare metal and semiconductor gauges, and show the bridge output and the errors that matter.
prereq: You need: the resistance-to-voltage idea from potentiometers and sensitivity and linearity from the static characteristics of sensors.

sections.h3: Strain, stress and the gauge factor

blocks.text: Stress σ is force per area, σ = F/A, with F in newtons and A in square metres; σ is in pascals (Pa). Strain ε is the fractional change in length, ε = ΔL/L, where ΔL is the change and L is the original length. Strain has no unit. It is often quoted in microstrain: 1 µε = 10⁻⁶. Young's modulus E = σ/ε connects the two for a linear elastic material; E is in Pa. Poisson's ratio ν is the magnitude of transverse strain divided by axial strain. A bar stretched along its axis also contracts sideways by ν times the axial strain.

blocks.where: GF is the gauge factor (dimensionless); R is the unstrained resistance in ohms (Ω); ΔR is the change in resistance in Ω; ε is the axial strain; ν is Poisson's ratio; ρ is resistivity in Ω·m and Δρ is its change. The first two terms, 1 + 2ν, are the geometric part; the last term is the piezoresistive part.

blocks.text: For a metal foil gauge the piezoresistive term is small, the geometric term dominates and GF is about 2. For a semiconductor gauge the piezoresistive term is large and GF can be 50 to 200. Some syllabi call GF the k-factor. A gauge factor of 2 means ΔR/R = 2ε. At ε = 500 µε, ΔR/R = 2 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.001, or 0.1 %.

By construction there are two families. An unbonded gauge stretches fine wires between a fixed frame and a moving armature; the wires carry the strain directly and form a bridge, as in early blood-pressure transducers. A bonded gauge is glued to the surface of the part and strains with it: a wire grid, an etched metal foil, or a semiconductor element.

A metal foil gauge uses a thin constantan foil, a copper-nickel alloy, etched into a grid and bonded to a polyimide backing. Constantan gives GF about 2, low temperature coefficient and good linearity. The grid is long and narrow so the gauge measures strain along one axis. Gauge lengths run from 0.2 mm to 100 mm. Short gauges fit small stress concentrations; long gauges average strain over a larger area. The backing is glued with cyanoacrylate after surface cleaning. Common resistances are 120 Ω and 350 Ω. Self-temperature-compensated alloys are matched to the test material's expansion so apparent strain is smaller.

A semiconductor gauge is a diffused silicon resistor formed on a silicon diaphragm or beam. Its GF is 50 to 200, so a small strain gives a large ΔR. The price is nonlinearity, a strong temperature coefficient and a smaller strain range. The sign of the piezoresistive term depends on doping type and crystal direction, so read the datasheet; do not assume the resistance always rises. Semiconductor gauges are common in MEMS pressure sensors (see the micro sensors).

Wire the gauge as one arm of a Wheatstone bridge. With one active gauge (quarter bridge) the output is V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε/4 for small strain (exactly V<sub>s</sub>·ΔR/(4R + 2ΔR)); with two active gauges at opposite strain (half bridge) it is V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε/2; with four (full bridge) V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε. V<sub>s</sub> is the bridge excitation voltage. Bridge balance and amplifiers come with signal conditioning.

Lead resistance adds to R and reduces sensitivity. Keep leads short and equal; in a quarter bridge, a long two-wire lead can also make the bridge unbalance. The datasheet's transverse sensitivity coefficient K<sub>t</sub> says how much strain perpendicular to the grid changes the reading; it matters in rosettes. Apparent strain is output with no load when temperature changes: the gauge expands differently from the part and its own resistance drifts. A dummy gauge, bonded to an unstrained piece of the same material and wired in the adjacent bridge arm, cancels much of this.

Three gauges at fixed angles form a rosette: rectangular at 0°, 45° and 90°, delta at 0°, 60° and 120°; the three readings give the principal strains and their directions. A gauge on a cantilever makes a displacement transducer: tip deflection δ bends the beam, and the surface strain at the root is ε = 3tδ/(2L²) for thickness t and length L (worked example 2). Gauges on a thin diaphragm make a pressure transducer: near the centre the surface is stretched, near the edge compressed, so two tangential and two radial gauges form a full bridge. The disposable blood-pressure transducer on every intensive-care monitor is this design, rated 5 µV/V/mmHg. Other biomedical uses: bone and implant strain, muscle-force and respiration belts. Force and torque from strain are in load cells and torque measurement.

examples.question: A constantan foil gauge has R = 120 Ω and gauge factor 2.0. It is bonded to a steel member carrying a strain of 500 µε. (a) Find ΔR. (b) Find the percentage change. (c) Repeat for a silicon gauge with gauge factor 100 at the same strain.
steps: For the metal gauge: ΔR = GF·ε·R = 2.0 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 120 Ω = 0.12 Ω.
For the silicon gauge: ΔR = 100 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 120 Ω = 6.0 Ω.
examples.answer: The metal gauge changes by 0.12 Ω (0.1 %); the silicon gauge changes by 6.0 Ω (5.0 %) at the same 500 µε strain.

examples.question: A steel cantilever 50 mm long and 1.0 mm thick carries one gauge on the top and one on the bottom surface at the root (GF = 2.0), wired as a half bridge at 5 V. Find the root strain and the bridge output for a tip deflection of 1.0 mm, and the sensitivity in mV/mm.
steps: The top gauge sees +600 µε (tension), the bottom −600 µε (compression); in adjacent arms their changes add.
Sensitivity = 3.0 mV per 1.0 mm = 3.0 mV/mm, linear while the beam stays elastic.
examples.answer: 600 µε at the root; 3.0 mV from the half bridge; 3.0 mV/mm.

traps: Dropping the 10⁻⁶: 500 µε is 500 × 10⁻⁶, not 500. A strain of 500 would be a 50,000 % length change, impossible for elastic metal.
Mixing ε and ΔL/L: ε is ΔL/L, so a 0.5 mm stretch on a 1 m bar is 500 µε, not 0.5 µε.
Treating GF as a resistance: GF is dimensionless. The same GF gives ΔR = GF·ε·R, so a 350 Ω gauge gives nearly three times the ΔR of a 120 Ω gauge at the same strain.
Assuming all semiconductor gauges have positive ΔR: doping type and crystal direction set the sign. Check the datasheet before wiring a bridge.
Forgetting transverse sensitivity and lead resistance in a rosette or quarter bridge: both shift the reading even when the axial strain is correct.

quiz.q: Define gauge factor and write its formula in terms of ΔR/R and ε.
quiz.a: GF = (ΔR/R)/ε. It is the fractional resistance change per unit axial strain and is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why is the gauge factor of a metal foil gauge close to 2, while a semiconductor gauge can exceed 100?
quiz.a: In metals the geometric term 1 + 2ν dominates and the resistivity change is small, so GF is about 2. In semiconductors the piezoresistive term (Δρ/ρ)/ε is large, so GF is 50 to 200.

quiz.q: A 350 Ω constantan gauge with GF = 2.1 is strained by 800 µε. Find ΔR and the percentage change.
A quarter bridge uses V<sub>s</sub> = 5 V, GF = 2.0 and ε = 1000 µε. Find the bridge output.
How does a dummy gauge reduce apparent strain? State the wiring condition.
quiz.a: Bond an unstrained gauge of the same type to the same material near the active gauge. Wire it in the adjacent bridge arm so temperature changes both resistances equally and the bridge subtracts the common change. It must see the same temperature but no mechanical strain.

quiz.q: Why is the full-bridge output for four active gauges four times the quarter-bridge output for one active gauge, for the same V<sub>s</sub>, GF and ε?
quiz.a: In a quarter bridge only one arm changes, giving V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε/4. In a full bridge all four arms change, and the bridge adds their contributions, giving V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε. The ratio is 4.

quiz.q: What is a strain rosette used for? Name two common layouts.
quiz.a: A rosette finds principal strains and their directions from three gauges at fixed angles. Rectangular: 0°, 45°, 90°. Delta: 0°, 60°, 120°.

beyond: Not for the exam. Thin-film gauges are now deposited directly on machine parts, and MEMS piezoresistive diaphragms put a full bridge on a silicon chip. Wearable and implantable versions measure breathing, gait and bone load outside the laboratory. Search for thin-film strain gauges and piezoresistive MEMS pressure sensors.
